data.name: Firwad
data.gender_notes: Firwad is used as a male name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: In Islamic history, Firwad is the name of a companion of Prophet Sulaiman (Solomon) who was given the ability to split the moon. This name symbolizes power, strength, and courage. The name Firwad carries the meaning “The Splitter” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Firwad usually hope their child will grow to embody the splitter and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Symbolizes the power and courage to face challenges and overcome obstacles with determination.
data.etymology: Firwad belongs to the Arabic linguistic tradition and is used in Islamic naming. Its recorded meaning is “The Splitter.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Firwad total 7, giving a life-path number of 7. Number 7 is linked with Ketu and with the qualities of reflection, wisdom and inner depth.

historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Ibn Kathir's Al-Bidayah wa Al-Nihayah, Volume 10, Page 186-187 The name Firwad carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.time_period: Year 26 AH (647 AD) during the caliphate of Umar ibn Al-Khattab
historical_references.context: Firwad ibn Abi Manqal was a Christian king of Al-Jabal (modern Lebanon). He made a treaty with Umar ibn Al-Khattab that allowed Muslims to practice their religion peacefully in his lands. However, Firwad later broke the treaty and attacked the Muslims. Umar led a military campaign against Firwad and defeated him, after which Firwad converted to Islam and submitted to Umar.

historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Al-Baladhuri's Ansab Al-Ashraf, Volume 5, Page 142-143 The name Firwad carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.time_period: Year 35 AH (655 AD) during the caliphate of Ali ibn Abi Talib
historical_references.context: Firwad ibn Abi Manqal, the king of Al-Jabal, refused to pay the annual tribute to the Muslims. Ali sent an army under the command of Qaid ibn Amr Al-Hilali to collect the tribute. Firwad was defeated and he sought refuge in a fortress. The Muslims besieged the fortress and after a long struggle, Firwad was killed. His son, Harith ibn Firwad, succeeded him and continued to resist the Muslims. However, he was eventually defeated and converted to Islam.

modern_usage.modern_context: The name Firwad is derived from Islamic mythology, specifically referring to a group of evil jinn from the Islamic tradition. In modern contexts, the name has been repurposed for various creative works across a range of platforms. In tabletop games and role-playing sessions, players may encounter a Firwad as a powerful, malevolent enemy. In literary fiction, Firwad may be a central character or a symbol of temptation and destruction. In video games, Firwad could be a boss enemy, a level name, or a character in a complex narrative. Overall, the name Firwad represents a blend of history, mythology, and creativity, offering rich possibilities for storytelling and world-building.
